content: Chronic cystic mastitis, also known as fibrocystic disease, diffuse cystic mastopathy, mammary dysplasia, fibrocystic disease of the breast, fibrocystic mastopathy, or fibroadenosis, is a condition rather than a disease. It is characterized by benign (noncancerous) changes in breast tissue, which may include irregular lumps or cysts, breast discomfort, sensitive nipples, and itching. These symptoms often fluctuate with the menstrual cycle and typically resolve after menopause. The exact causes of chronic cystic mastitis are not fully understood, but they are closely linked to ovarian hormone levels, as the condition usually subsides after menopause. It is also associated with the menstrual cycle and dietary factors. Women who use birth control pills tend to have a lower incidence of this condition, likely due to the regulation of hormone levels. Additionally, dietary fat levels, caffeine intake, and family history may influence the development of the condition. Certain medications, such as clomifene, may also contribute as a side effect. Epidemiologically, it is estimated that 30-60% of women experience this condition, which is marked by noncancerous lumps in the breast. The natural history of chronic cystic mastitis is generally benign, with no significant adverse side effects. In nearly all cases, the condition resolves after menopause. However, a potential complication is that cancerous tumors may be more challenging to detect in women with this condition due to the presence of irregular breast tissue. Symptoms of chronic cystic mastitis include breast discomfort, sensitive nipples, and itching. These symptoms follow a periodic pattern closely tied to the menstrual cycle, peaking just before menstruation and subsiding afterward. During peak symptoms, the breasts may feel full and swollen. Importantly, no complications related to breastfeeding have been identified. On physical examination, the condition is characterized by the presence of fibrous tissue and a lumpy, cobblestone texture in the breasts. The lumps are typically smooth, with well-defined edges, and are usually mobile relative to surrounding structures. However, these lumps may sometimes be obscured by irregularities in the breast tissue associated with the condition. The lumps are most commonly found in the upper, outer sections of the breast, near the armpit. Women with this condition may experience persistent or intermittent aching in their breasts due to periodic swelling. The breasts and nipples may also be tender or itchy. Mammography is often not effective for diagnosing chronic cystic mastitis because the breast tissue is frequently too dense for thorough examination. Diagnosis is usually straightforward for a physician but may occasionally require a biopsy of the affected area. There is no definitive cure for chronic cystic mastitis. However, symptoms can often be managed by reducing caffeine and fat intake and wearing a well-fitting bra. In severe cases, a synthetic androgen may be prescribed. For larger cysts, aspiration using a very fine needle can be performed to drain fluid.
